meta.title: The Light at the Harbor
meta.skill_frame: Find the main idea: decide what a whole passage is mostly about, not one true detail.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fifth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 7.4 on the three parts together, inside the grade 4-5 band. The load is a message reduced to two choices, then a reason the state paid for it.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from NOAA Ocean Service, 'Do We Still Need Lighthouses?'
source.attribution: U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, Ocean Service, 'Do We Still Need Lighthouses?', https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/lighthouse.html, accessed 2026-11-15. U.S. federal government work; public domain in the U.S.
source.text_status: Adapted, reading load reduced by splitting long sentences.
source.survey: A lighthouse gives one plain message at a place where a wrong turn is dangerous, which is why the government took the job on first.
source.avoided: No claim that lighthouses are obsolete; no chart details.

session.difficulty_basis: How far the stated idea sits from the words the passage uses.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Lighthouses and beacons are towers. They have bright lights and fog horns. They stand at important or dangerous places. Some stand on rocky cliffs. Some stand on sandy shoals on land. Others stand on wave-swept reefs in the sea. They can also be found at entrances to harbors and bays. These places are on land, in the sea, and at harbor entrances. These long-trusted navigation aids warn sailors of dangerous shallows. They warn them of dangerous rocky coasts. They also help guide boats safely into and out of harbors. Their messages are simple. They say either stay away, danger, beware, or come this way.
passage.part_2: On August 7, 1789, Congress approved the Lighthouse Act. It was the first public works program undertaken by the new federal government. The act established and supported lighthouses, beacons, buoys, and public piers. August 7 is recognized as National Lighthouse Day. The Lighthouse Act was approved on August 7, 1789. Congress approved this first public works program. The new federal government undertook the program. The act established and supported lighthouses. It also established and supported beacons, buoys, and public piers. August 7 is National Lighthouse Day. The act was approved by Congress. This program was undertaken by the new federal government.
passage.part_3: Even with the arrival of advanced navigation technology, many lighthouses still sparkle for seafarers. Many lighthouses still shine. Cartographers in NOAA's Office of Coast Survey practice the art and science of designing, compiling, updating, and distributing electronic navigational charts. These charts are specifically tailored to the needs of marine navigation. The charts are made for marine navigation. Cartographers are mapmakers. They practice this art and science. Mapmakers design them. They compile them. They update them. They distribute them. These electronic charts are made for the needs of marine navigation. Many lighthouses still shine for seafarers. Advanced navigation technology exists, but many lighthouses still sparkle.
